title: 13. Spatial data in R

Once again we'll play catch-up by running through some of the
[notes](https://bldgspatialdata.github.io/website/) from GES 668, Building
Spatial Datasets. Most of our spatial data will be in data types that come from
the `sf` package, but we'll also use `terra` for raster data a bit. Other
resources:

- The [`sf`](https://r-spatial.github.io/sf/) and
  [`terra`](https://rspatial.github.io/terra/) package docs (both include
  cheatsheets)
- The slides from Building Spatial Datasets, particularly [week
  2](https://bldgspatialdata.github.io/website/slides/spatial-data.html#/how-does-r-work-with-spatial-data)
  (start on section 3)
- @lovelace2025, especially [chapter 2](https://r.geocompx.org/spatial-class)
  for an overview of packages and data types
- Stack Overflow's [r-sf](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/tagged/r-sf) tag

## Types of spatial data

What type of spatial data you have will affect what you can do with it and how
you go about mapping it. The main types are:

- **Point data**, where observations are characterized by their location. These
  points might also have attributes associated with them.
- **Grid data**, where measurements are taken at locations distributed
  throughout an area. These don't need to be on a strict square grid; values
  might be interpolated between measured locations. **Rasters** are a common
  form of this where observations *are* more or less taken on a grid, often
  represented as one pixel per location (either observed or interpolated).
- **Areal data**, where values are associated with two-dimensional regions.
  These are often based on man-made boundaries such as countries, towns, etc.

We'll be working with areal data the most. It has some drawbacks as far as
visualizing data that we'll talk about, but it is also flexible. For example, we
have easy access to tract boundaries that cover all of Maryland. We have lots of
data associated with each of those tracts. We can also join those tract
geographies with other spatial data, including points within the tracts or
overlaps between tracts and some other area. We can convert from that areal data
to other data types, although we'll lose some information (interpolating values
associated with census tracts to a square grid, representing tracts as their
centroids instead). Or we can aggregate point or grid data to areal boundaries
(count of points within each polygon, pixels apportioned to polygons).

## Spatial data in R

### The spatial ecosystem

A few packages to install first (cross your fingers because the dependencies can
be tough):

```{r}
#| label: spatial-setup
#| eval: false
#| include: true

pkgs <- c(
    "sf", # sf : spatial data :: dplyr : tabular data
    "osmdata", # batch download data from OpenStreetMap
    "terra", # sf-friendly raster tools
    "tigris", # download shapefiles from the Census Bureau TIGER database
    "rmapshaper", # command line tool to edit geographies
    "tidyterra" # dplyr functions + ggplot geoms for terra rasters
)

install.packages(pkgs)

# or pak::pkg_install(pkgs)
```

Much of the R spatial ecosystem has migrated from an older set of packages
(`sp`, `rgeos`, `rgdal`) to a newer one (`sf`, plus its friends like `stars` and
`terra`) designed to fit into the tidyverse packages.^[This was actually a major
[concerted effort](https://r-spatial.org/r/2022/04/12/evolution.html) over the
past few years because the original maintainer of many of those packages was
retiring.] `sf` is also nice because many of the functions are based on PostGIS,
so if you've worked with spatial databases (or might in the future) it's easy to
translate code.

There are a few `sf`-based datasets in the justviz package, and many others are
easy to get (`tigris` is very easy to use for Census Bureau data, and we'll use
`osmdata` to get OpenStreetMap shapefiles and data).

`sf` objects can be data frames with a geometry column, so you can work with
them in many of the same ways as regular data frames; you might also see just
plain geometry objects without any data attached.

### Plotting

#### Vector geometries (e.g. points & polygons)

`sf` is the main package we'll use for handling vector geometries, such as points, lines, polygons, etc.`sf` objects have a `plot` method, so you can just call
`plot(very_cool_sf_data)` and get a basic plot:

```{r}
#| label: map-base
#| message: false

library(sf)
library(ggplot2)

head(justviz::tracts_sf)

# just showing county column
plot(justviz::tracts_sf[, "county"])
```

::: {.aside}
A note about object-oriented programming (OOP): When you have a function that's
a method of some type of object, just as `plot`, you can look at help pages for
that function by specifying the object type. So `?plot.sf` will show you the
docs for `plot` as it applies specifically to `sf` objects.
:::

ggplot also has geoms for spatial data. For these notes, we'll mostly just use
`sf`'s plot method to focus on spatial data types, not mapping.

```{r}
#| label: map-gg

ggplot(justviz::tracts_sf) +
    geom_sf(aes(fill = county))
```

#### Raster geometries

Rasters are made up of grids with some set of attributes at each grid square. For example, if you're studying tree canopy, you might have a grid of the state divided into 30m x 30m cells or pixels. For each cell, you might have a categorical attribute like main land cover type (is this cell mostly covered by grass, trees, water, impervious surfaces, etc). Or you might have just true/false data for whether the cells is mostly tree canopy. Or you might have a continuous numeric measurement, like the percentage of the cell that is covered by trees. The bottom line is you have a set resolution for the data, and you have some attribute(s) for each of those cells. There's a dataset in `justviz` of landcover raster data; because of its size, you need a separate function to load it into your session. (I fixed a bug in how the dataset is read, so you need package version **0.3.1**.)

There are two major packages that handle raster data and are made to be compatible with `sf`: `stars`, made by the same developers as `sf` (the r-spatial crew), and `terra`, made to more directly carry on older packages from the `sp` world (the rspatial crew).

We're not doing a ton with raster data, and while `stars` has syntax more similar to `sf`, it also has bigger aims than we need (storing time series spatial data as cubes). So we'll use `terra` with the `tidyterra` package unless someone has a pressing need to do otherwise.


```{r}
#| label: raster-1
land <- justviz::load_land_cover()

land
```

From the object's printout you can see it's got a resolution of 30m x 30m with 1 layer. We can plot it with `terra`'s plot method using a color table that's stored in the raster data.

::: {.aside}
This dataset is cropped to the same extent as the tracts shapefile. If you need to work with the same data for a different area, see the code that preps the data in the [`justviz` package](https://github.com/umbc-viz/justviz/blob/main/data-raw/landcover.R)
:::

```{r}
#| label: raster-plot
terra::plot(land)
```

Use `terra::mask` to filter a `SpatRaster` object. You can also use `tidyterra::filter` to get `dplyr`-like syntax, but it seems to drop the landcover color table.

```{r}
#| label: raster-tidy
library(terra)
forest <- terra::mask(
  land,
  land %in% c("Mixed Forest", "Evergreen Forest", "Deciduous Forest"),
  maskvalues = FALSE
)
plot(forest)
```


### Projections

Just like in desktop GIS software, in R you can reproject spatial data to
different coordinate reference systems (CRS). This is easiest if your data
already has a CRS attached to it (all the datasets in `justviz` do, as do any
you download from the Census Bureau with the `tigris` package, and many others).
In some cases, mostly if you're creating a bit of spatial data manually, you'll
need to first assign a CRS explicitly, then transform.

Some CRS codes you'll see often:

- [EPSG:4269](https://spatialreference.org/ref/epsg/4269/), default for data
  downloaded from the Census Bureau
- [EPSG:3857](https://spatialreference.org/ref/epsg/3857/), aka Web Mercator
- [EPSG:4326](https://spatialreference.org/ref/epsg/4326/), used most often in
  GPS
- [EPSG:2248](https://spatialreference.org/ref/epsg/2248/), projected for good
  views of Maryland with units in feet

That last one is useful for us making maps locally because 1) it makes Maryland
look pretty, and 2) having units in feet makes it easier to do transformations
or calculations based on distances.

Locally, you probably won't see much difference between these CRSes, but you
would for a map of a large portion of the country.

```{r}
#| label: md-crs
#| echo: false

# datasets in base R
state_info <- data.frame(state = state.abb, region = state.region)
states_sf <- tigris::states(cb = TRUE, progress_bar = FALSE) |>
    dplyr::select(state = STUSPS) |>
    dplyr::inner_join(state_info, by = "state") |>
    dplyr::filter(region == "South")

transform_map <- function(df, lbl, crs = NULL) {
    if (!is.null(crs)) {
        df <- sf::st_transform(df, crs)
    } else {
        crs <- sf::st_crs(df)$epsg
    }
    ggplot(df) +
        geom_sf() +
        labs(title = stringr::str_glue("EPSG:{crs}, {lbl}"))
}

purrr::walk(
    list(
        list(lbl = "Census", crs = NULL),
        list(lbl = "web mercator", crs = 3857),
        list(lbl = "revolves around MD, uses feet", crs = 2248),
        list(lbl = "US equal area", crs = 9311)
    ),
    function(map_meta) {
        p <- transform_map(states_sf, map_meta[["lbl"]], map_meta[["crs"]])
        print(p)
    }
)
```

## Things to do with spatial data

Because `sf` is designed to be compatible with the tidyverse packages, you can
do many of the same things to `sf` data frames as you can to regular ones. When
you plot `sf` data frames or other objects with ggplot, you can also layer the
spatial geoms like you would other geoms.

### Aggregating spatial data

The most basic way to aggregate spatial data is to just take your geometries and
squish them all together. You might do this to save space & memory if you have a
very large set of points and only need locations, not any individual points'
attributes. You also might do it to make smaller geometries into bigger ones.
This is helpful in mapping hierarchical shapes, because sometimes shapes will be
slightly different from one object to the next and you end up with tracts that
are supposed to fit inside towns but have tiny gaps in some places that make
your map look janky and unprofessional. When possible, I prefer starting with my
smallest geography and aggregating up to larger ones.

In order to save space, I put a shapefile in `justviz` of tracts but not
counties, because you can aggregate up to counties. `sf` lets you do this in the
same way as you would with other `dplyr`-based summarization. You can use a
function inside `dplyr::summarise` like you normally would (e.g. mean, median,
etc), or you can leave the summarization empty to just get the combined
geometries.

```{r}
#| label: aggregate

# grouped by county
counties_sf <- justviz::tracts_sf |>
  dplyr::group_by(county) |>
  dplyr::summarise()

plot(counties_sf[, "county"])

# no grouping
region_sf <- justviz::tracts_sf |>
  dplyr::summarise()

plot(region_sf)
```

### Joining spatial & nonspatial data

You can join spatial data frames and nonspatial data frames the same way you
would [join](../extras/joining_data.qmd) two regular (nonspatial) data frames. I
generally keep the spatial data frame on the left for two reasons:

- The data type follows from the table on the left side of the join. That means
  if you join an sf data frame on the left and a regular one on the right,
  you'll get back an `sf` data frame; if you join a regular data frame on the
  left and an `sf` one on the right, you'll get a regular data frame that
  happens to have a geometry column.
- If I'm making a map, I most likely want every relevant geometry (e.g. every
  tract in the city) even if I have some areas that don't have data. You can
  ensure that you'll have all the shapes even if they don't have data if you put
  your spatial data on the left side of the join, and use a left join rather
  than an inner join.

However, if you do an operation that returns a nonspatial data frame that has a
valid geometry column, you can get it back into an `sf` data type with
`sf::st_as_sf`, which coerces `sf`-related data types. Here are some examples
related to joining tracts in Baltimore city with incomplete tract-level data.
Let's say we're mapping an analysis related to housing in the city, but we only
want to study tracts with at least 1000 households.

```{r}
#| label: join-1

balt_sf <- justviz::tracts_sf |> dplyr::filter(county == "Baltimore city")

balt_housing <- justviz::acs |>
  dplyr::mutate(is_in_housing_study = total_hh >= 1000) |>
  dplyr::filter(county == "Baltimore city", is_in_housing_study) |>
  dplyr::select(county, name, total_hh, is_in_housing_study)

paste0("class of balt_sf: ", toString(class(balt_sf)))
paste0("class of balt_housing: ", toString(class(balt_housing)))

# if you run this in a console, you'll see information about the geometries
balt_housing_sf <- balt_sf |>
  dplyr::left_join(balt_housing, by = c("county", "geoid" = "name"))
head(balt_housing_sf) # 199 rows

# if you run this in a console, you *won't* see info about the geometries
balt_housing_df <- balt_housing |>
  dplyr::left_join(balt_sf, by = c("county", "name" = "geoid"))
head(balt_housing_df) # 118 rows

plot(balt_housing_sf[, "is_in_housing_study"])

# get balt_housing_df back to sf data frame to do the same
plot(sf::st_as_sf(balt_housing_df)[, "is_in_housing_study"])
```

### Transforming spatial data

There are lots of ways to transform spatial data, and the `sf`
[docs](https://r-spatial.github.io/sf/articles/sf3.html) and
[books](https://r.geocompx.org/geometry-operations#geo-vec) go into a lot of
detail on them. Some that we'll use for making maps in this class are:

- **simplification**, removing vertices from lines or boundaries
- **buffers**, expanding or contracting a geometry by a set amount
- **centroids**, center of mass of a polygon
- **intersections**, geometries created as the combination of shapes in both of
  a set of geometries

### Spatial predicates and joins

Predicates are functions that return true/false. Think of them as asking, for
each pair of geometries, questions like is point A inside polygon B, or is
polygon C contained entirely within polygon D, or does shape E intersect with
shape F in any way? Because these can be used for *spatial joins*, there's a
convenient list of them at `?sf::st_join`. I most often use `sf::st_intersects`,
which is the default for spatial joins and just determines whether 2 shapes of
whatever dimensions touch in some way. A point and line can intersect, a line
and polygon can intersect, 2 polygons can intersect, etc.

Once you know *how* you want to join two sets of geometries, a spatial join will
combine them based on your predicate function. These follow some of the same
mechanisms as other table joins, such as whether it is a left join or inner
join.

I most commonly use spatial joins to locate points inside polygons, such as
assigning each of Baltimore's public artworks to a census tract:

```{r}
#| label: art-points

head(justviz::art_sf)
summary(justviz::art_sf)

justviz::art_sf |>
  sf::st_join(justviz::tracts_sf) |>
  head()
```

Note that there are 672 points in the art dataset, and now 672 points in the
joined dataset. Like with joins between an `sf` data frame and a regular one,
the geometry type follows the data frame on the left^[I imagine it's possible
for there to be edge cases where this isn't true, but AFAIK it's generally
true.]. I think about it as the left data frame being the one I'm most
interested in holding on to, and the right is the one that's providing
additional attributes. In this case, I'm studying artworks and want to add tract
to the set of information I have on each.

If instead I were interested in tracts, and wanted to know what types of artwork
or how many pieces were in each tract, I could switch the order around:

```{r}
#| label: art-polys

justviz::tracts_sf |>
  sf::st_join(justviz::art_sf) |>
  head()
```

Here's one use of this: the art dataset comes from Baltimore's open data portal,
but for whatever reason a few points are outside the city. Say we wanted to
limit this to just pieces that are strictly inside the city (and pretend the
data didn't have a county column). You can filter tracts for just the city, then
do an inner join to attach that to the art locations.

```{r}
#| label: art-join

justviz::art_sf |>
  # left = FALSE turns this from a left join to an inner join
  sf::st_join(balt_sf, left = FALSE) |>
  head()
```

Now this is cut down from the original 672 points to 661.

Note also that to do any sort of spatial operation between two objects, they
need the same CRS. In this case, I built the datasets to have the same CRS from
the start, but you'll often need to decided on one and reproject the shapes.

## Getting spatial data

One of the tough things about working with spatial data is the system
dependencies such as drivers that can be hard to have all in alignment. One of
the nicest things about `sf` is how easily it can read different spatial data
types. Some common types are Esri shapefiles (.shp), GeoPackage (.gpkg), and
GeoJSON (.json or .geojson)---the last one is especially common with data coming
from APIs. Raster data usually comes in pixel-based formats like GeoTIFF (.tif)
or netCDF (.cdf). You shouldn't have any trouble opening valid files in these
formats with either `sf` or `terra`.

There are also packages to help read data directly from ArcGIS services into
`sf` data frames, such as
[`arcgislayers`](https://github.com/R-ArcGIS/arcgislayers), maintained in part
by our friend Eli. This is how I got data from local open data portals into
`justviz`.

The Census Bureau has downloads of official geographies through the TIGER
program, some of which are updated routinely (tracts get redrawn after each
decennial census, legislative districts get redrawn and gerrymandered, OMB
changes metro area definitions. I'm still fixing definitions of things from when
Connecticut abolished counties in 2022). These are online as shapefiles, but the
easiest way to access them in R is the
[`tigris`](https://github.com/walkerke/tigris) package, which lets you pick
geography types, subsets, and years to download, optionally stashing them in
your computer's cache, and reads them as `sf` data frames.

You might also encounter spatial databases, such as PostGIS, or databases like
SQLite or duckdb with spatial extensions. `sf`'s functions are named to mirror
PostGIS, so if and when you need to work with spatial databases, you'll be
fairly familiar with the operations.^[`dplyr`was also designed to, at least in
part, mirror SQL verbs.]

There's a lot more detail in @lovelace2025 ch. 8 and 10.7.
